summary: Defines extra L2TPv3 bit values in the Circuit Status AVP to report finer-grained error states for attachment circuits and pseudowires. It also generalizes the Active bit and deprecates the use of the New bit in the Circuit Status AVP.

plainLanguage.summary:
L2TPv3 could already say whether a circuit was up or down. This RFC adds bits that say where the fault is and whether the circuit is a standby that is ready but not carrying traffic.

It also tightens up the old bits, so that an old and a new implementation still agree about what the status means.

questions: what is the l2tpv3 circuit status avp
what does the n bit mean in l2tpv3
what are l2tpv3 fault status bits
subtitle: More bits in the L2TPv3 status field, so a fault says which direction and which end failed.

tldr.problem: The L2TPv3 Circuit Status AVP could say only whether a circuit was up or down, which does not tell an operator which direction the fault is in or whether the pseudowire is a standby.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC widens the two-byte status field with four fault bits, one for each direction and each end, adds a standby bit, redefines the Active bit to cover the whole local endpoint, and deprecates the New bit.
tldr.outcome: The new bits apply to every pseudowire type that uses the Circuit Status AVP, and the five RFCs that define the old bits are updated to match. The document is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5641 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates the Circuit Status definitions in RFC 3931 and in the four pseudowire type documents RFC 4349, RFC 4454, RFC 4591 and RFC 4719, so those documents now carry the extended status bits and the deprecation of the New bit.

sections.title: Why a Finer Circuit Status
sections.content:
The L2TPv3 Circuit Status AVP can already report whether an access circuit is up or down. The RFC says a finer granularity is often useful, because it tells an operator which direction the fault is in. The same idea has already been added for MPLS-based pseudowires, where the pseudowire control protocol using the Label Distribution Protocol carries it.

A second case is session-level redundancy. There it is useful to be able to indicate that a pseudowire is in a standby state: fully established by signalling and available for operations, administration and maintenance, but not switching data. That function is available for MPLS-based pseudowires using LDP as well.

This document provides extended circuit status bit values for L2TPv3 and adds them in a way that stays backwards compatible with the current Circuit Status AVP. The new bits apply to all pseudowire types that use the Circuit Status AVP.
sections.plainLanguage: L2TPv3 could already say whether a circuit was up or down. This RFC adds bits that say where the fault is and whether the circuit is a standby that is ready but not carrying traffic.

sections.title: Abbreviations
sections.content:
The RFC uses a short set of names for the parts of an L2TPv3 setup: AC for the attachment circuit, AVP for the attribute value pair, LCCE for the L2TP control connection endpoint, NNI for the network-network interface, PE for the provider edge, PSN for the packet switched network and PW for the pseudowire. The L2TPv3 control message types are listed in Section 6 of RFC 3931.

The document then works with the two sides of a tunnel. The local pseudowire endpoint is described as including the local attachment circuit and the local PSN-facing pseudowire termination, so a fault can be placed either on the customer-facing circuit or in the direction of the packet switched network, and the status bits say which.
sections.plainLanguage: The short names matter because the status bits distinguish the customer-facing circuit from the network-facing end of the tunnel.

sections.title: The Extended Status Bitmap
sections.content:
The Circuit Status AVP, Attribute Type 71, appears in the ICRQ, ICRP, ICCN, OCRQ, OCRP, OCCN and SLI control messages. It indicates the initial status of the circuit the session is bound to, or a change in that status. Its Attribute Value field is two bytes. RFC 3931 defined it with a Reserved field and two bits: bit 15, value 0x0001, the Active bit, which said whether the circuit was up, active or ready (1) or down, inactive or not ready (0), and bit 14, value 0x0002, the New bit, which said whether the status indication was for a new circuit (1) or an existing circuit (0).

The Active bit

The Active bit now indicates whether the local pseudowire endpoint, which includes the local attachment circuit and the local PSN-facing pseudowire termination, has no faults present and is up, active or ready (1), or has faults present and is down, inactive or not ready (0).

The New bit

The New bit keeps its meaning but is deprecated. It was provided to emulate network-network interface signalling between provider edge routers, for example Frame Relay NNI. It MAY be used to convey that a circuit has been re-provisioned or newly provisioned at the provider edge, which can already be inferred from the type of the L2TP control message, so the RFC says it is uncertain what the receiving provider edge can make of the bit, although it MAY include logging. The bit SHOULD be ignored on receipt and is OPTIONAL to set on sending.

The four fault bits

Four new bits say where a fault is. Together they are called the fault status bits.

  • R, bit 13, value 0x0004, local attachment circuit (ingress) receive fault: an alarm or fault has occurred at the local attachment circuit such that it is unable to receive traffic. It can still transmit traffic.
  • T, bit 12, value 0x0008, local attachment circuit (egress) transmit fault: a fault has occurred at the local attachment circuit such that it is unable to transmit traffic. It can still receive traffic.
  • I, bit 11, value 0x0010, local PSN-facing pseudowire (ingress) receive fault: a fault has occurred in the receive direction between the local endpoint and the remote L2TP endpoint.
  • E, bit 10, value 0x0020, local PSN-facing pseudowire (egress) transmit fault: a fault has occurred in the transmit direction between the local endpoint and the remote L2TP endpoint.

For the two bits that describe the direction between the endpoints, the RFC notes that a fault at session level would not necessarily trigger an L2TP control connection timeout. How such a fault is detected is out of scope; it might be by pseudowire type-specific means, by Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, or by other methods.

The standby bit

The last new bit, S, bit 9, value 0x0040, says the pseudowire is in Standby mode. That means it was signalled during setup of the pseudowire and is operational, but it is not switching user traffic. Any received user traffic SHOULD be dropped, and user traffic MUST NOT be transmitted.

A standby pseudowire also allows the data plane liveness to be checked, so that it is known to be able to switch data packets end to end. This can be done as described in RFC 5085, or with Bidirectional Forwarding Detection for the pseudowire virtual circuit connectivity verification. Even so, data is not forwarded from an attachment circuit into the L2TPv3 session, or from the L2TPv3 session out to the attachment circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: The status is a two-byte field of bits. This RFC gives one bit a wider meaning, adds four bits for the four possible fault directions, adds a bit for standby, and marks the old New bit as no longer worth using.

sections.title: How the Bits Combine
sections.content:
In implementations that predate this specification, bits 0 to 13 MUST be set to zero, as Section 5.4.5 of RFC 3931 requires. That is what allows a legacy implementation to interwork properly with a new one.

The RFC then clarifies how the bits are used.

  • The R, T, I and E bits are collectively referred to as the fault status bits.
  • RFC 3931 defined the Active bit as pertaining to the local access circuit state only. This document redefines it as meaning that no faults are present on the local pseudowire endpoint.
  • If multiple faults occur, all the fault status bits corresponding to each fault MUST be set, that is, they MUST be bitwise ORed together.
  • The Active bit MUST NOT be set until all the fault status bits are cleared. That behaviour lets an endpoint stay compatible with a remote endpoint that does not understand the new status bits.
  • If any of the fault status bits are set, the Active bit MUST be cleared. The fault status bits are a more granular definition of the Active bit, so that ORing them gives an inverted Active.
  • If the Active bit is clear and the fault status bits are clear, there is no extended circuit status: the circuit is down, inactive or not ready, without a finer indication.
  • The Standby bit can be set in conjunction with any other bit, including Active. A pseudowire endpoint in standby can be up, active or ready, or it can be experiencing a fault.
  • Leaving standby mode is indicated by the clearing of the Standby bit.
  • The usage of the New bit has been deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules keep old and new equipment working together. When something goes wrong the fault bits are set and the Active bit is cleared; when everything is fine again the fault bits are cleared first and only then is Active set. The standby bit can sit alongside any of the others.

sections.title: Updates to Existing RFCs
sections.content:
The document updates five existing RFCs that define, either generically or for a specific set of pseudowire types, the Active and New bits of the Circuit Status AVP. Section 5.4.5 of RFC 3931 defines them, and the definitions are replicated in Section 3.4 of RFC 4349 (High-Level Data Link Control frames over L2TPv3), Section 8 of RFC 4454 (Asynchronous Transfer Mode over L2TPv3), Section 3.4 of RFC 4591 (Frame Relay over L2TPv3) and Section 2.3.3 of RFC 4719 (Ethernet frames over L2TPv3). All five now carry the new wording for the Active bit and the deprecation of the New bit.

Two sentences are removed from Section 2.2 of RFC 4719. They said that for ICRQ and ICRP the Circuit Status AVP MUST indicate that the circuit status is for a new circuit, and that for ICCN and SLI it MUST indicate that the circuit status is for an existing circuit and reflect the current status of the link.

Finally, Section 3.1 of RFC 4349, Section 3.1 of RFC 4454, Section 3.1 of RFC 4591 and Section 2.2 of RFC 4719 receive an added paragraph, saying that because the use of the New bit is deprecated, the AVP need not indicate on sending, nor check on receipt, that the circuit status is for a new circuit or for an existing circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: Five earlier documents defined the same two bits, so this RFC changes all five at once. The practical effect for an operator is that the new and the old bits now mean the same thing everywhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security considerations for the Circuit Status AVP are covered in the base L2TPv3 specification, in Section 8 of RFC 3931. The RFC states that no additional security considerations exist with extending this attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new here. The security rules for the L2TPv3 base protocol already cover this attribute.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The Circuit Status Bits number space is managed by IANA as set out in Section 10.7 of RFC 3931. Five new bits, bits 9 through 13, and one updated bit, bit 14, have been assigned. Bit 9 is the S (Standby) bit, bit 10 the E bit for a local PSN-facing pseudowire egress transmit fault, bit 11 the I bit for a local PSN-facing pseudowire ingress receive fault, bit 12 the T bit for a local attachment circuit egress transmit fault, bit 13 the R bit for a local attachment circuit ingress receive fault, and bit 14 the N (New) bit, whose use is deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: The bits were given fixed places in the two-byte field, so that every implementation reads them in the same positions.

viz.caption: CIRCUIT STATUS AVP ATTRIBUTE VALUE (RFC 5641 SECTION 2)

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Unused. Implementations before this specification set bits 0 to 13 to zero.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: The pseudowire is in Standby mode: signalled and operational, but not switching user traffic.

fields.name: N
fields.desc: New. Deprecated: ignore on receipt, optional to set on sending.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Pseudowire has no faults: the local endpoint is up, active and ready.

cells: Cannot receive traffic, can still transmit
Cannot transmit traffic, can still receive
Local and remote endpoint, receive direction
A fault in the receive direction
Local and remote endpoint, transmit direction
A fault in the transmit direction

viz.caption: RULES FOR COMBINING THE STATUS BITS

items.title: Faults come first
items.text: The Active bit MUST NOT be set until every fault status bit is cleared.

items.title: Several faults at once
items.text: All the fault status bits for each fault are set together, bitwise ORed.

items.title: No detail
items.text: Active clear and all fault bits clear means down, with no finer reason.

items.title: Standby is independent
items.text: The Standby bit can be set together with any other bit, including Active.

items.title: New is deprecated
items.text: The New bit should be ignored on receipt and is optional to set on sending.
